sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13

items.sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13:1
items.html: The meaning is that in the ten Sefirot of reflected light that emerge from the coupling of striking, called Observation, Malchut — which is the secret of the mouth, called "Et" — is found to be the root of the ten Sefirot of reflected light. And therefore it follows that whatever is more attached to its root, namely to the phase of the Malchut that is in the mouth, is more important and higher, since it is from her that the reflected light is drawn and issues from below upward, as written above.

items.sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13:2
items.html: The meaning is that in the ten Sefirot of direct light, Keter, which is adjacent to the eye, is found to be the one that emerged first and is the root of all ten Sefirot of direct light, and its stature is regarded as higher than all of them. However, in the ten Sefirot of reflected light that emerge through Observation in Malchut, the opposite is found: the Malchut that is in the mouth becomes the root of the ten Sefirot of reflected light, and she gives the light to all ten Sefirot. Thus Yesod is found second in rank, and Hod third, and so on until Keter adjacent to the eye, which is the last to receive. And this is what he means by saying that Keter adjacent to the eye emerged last, meaning that it is the last recipient of the expansion of the reflected light from Malchut.

items.sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13:3
items.html: The meaning is that since, from the side of direct light, Keter is found first in rank and Malchut last in rank, because she is the last to receive and is furthest from the root; whereas from the side of the expansion of reflected light the opposite is found, that the Sefira of Malchut was the root and is first in rank while Keter is last — it follows that by force of the clothing of the reflected light within the direct light, all the vessels become equal in one and the same stature. For whatever is more praiseworthy in the ten Sefirot of direct light is regarded as more deficient in the ten Sefirot of reflected light, and conversely, whatever is more praiseworthy in the ten Sefirot of reflected light is regarded as more deficient in the ten Sefirot of direct light. Thus all the phases of the vessels are found equal, and understand this.

items.sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13:4
items.html: The meaning is that through the reflected light that emerged from Malchut from below upward, all the Sefirot expanded and rose in equal stature up to Keter adjacent to the eye, as above. However, all this is on account of the Malchut that is in the mouth, as above. And this is what he means by saying that Yesod expands more inward — meaning that although it is found more inward than Malchut, since Malchut clothes upon it from without as is known, nonetheless this is not considered a superiority, because its entire expansion up to Keter comes about by the power of Malchut, so that Malchut is the root of this expansion of its stature and of this its merit. And this is what he means in saying that Yesod, from the abundance of Malchut's light, had the power to expand further — meaning that the reflected light of Malchut caused it to expand in stature beyond its measure in the ten Sefirot of direct light. Therefore it is not more praiseworthy than its own root, which is Malchut.

items.sefariaRef: Ohr Penimi on Talmud Eser HaSefirot 3:13:5
items.html: The meaning is that nonetheless there is certainly a superiority of Yesod over Malchut, for the entire merit of Malchut is only in the phase of reflected light alone, whereas Yesod is preferable to her since it precedes in the ten Sefirot of direct light, which is far preferable to reflected light, as is known. However this is only with regard to the lights alone; but with regard to the vessels themselves, their essence is only from reflected light, and this is what he means in saying that with regard to the vessels themselves they are equal, for the measure of stature and the merit of the vessels are drawn only from reflected light, and understand this. See in Part 1, Panim Meirot uMasbirot, Branch 3, where all this is explained at length.
